questions.q: Without TRY/CATCH, what happens when a runtime error occurs mid-script?
options: The error is silently ignored
SQL Server automatically retries the statement
The rest of the script runs normally, skipping only the failed line
The batch stops at that point, and the error propagates up to whatever called it
questions.explain: This is exactly the problem TRY/CATCH exists to let you handle gracefully.

questions.q: What happens the instant an error occurs inside a TRY block?
options: The error is logged but execution continues in TRY as normal
The whole script terminates immediately with no further processing
CATCH runs first, then TRY resumes
Execution jumps immediately to the CATCH block, skipping whatever remained in TRY
questions.explain: The remainder of the TRY block never executes once an error is caught.

questions.q: What does ERROR_MESSAGE() return when called outside a CATCH block?
options: NULL
An empty string
It causes a syntax error
The most recent error from any prior script
questions.explain: ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), and ERROR_LINE() are only meaningful inside a CATCH block.

questions.q: Why should ROLLBACK live inside the CATCH block when combining TRY/CATCH with a transaction?
options: It guarantees atomicity even in the face of an unexpected error, rather than leaving a partial change behind
It has no functional purpose there — it's purely a style choice
ROLLBACK cannot be used anywhere except inside CATCH
It prevents the CATCH block from running at all
questions.explain: This ties Lessons 72, 73, and 76 together — CATCH is exactly where you'd handle an unexpected failure mid-transaction.

questions.q: If no error occurs inside a TRY block, does the matching CATCH block ever run?
options: Only on the first execution of the script
Yes, CATCH always runs regardless of whether an error occurred
No — CATCH only runs when an error actually occurs inside TRY
Only if the TRY block contains a transaction
questions.explain: CATCH is purely error-triggered — a successful TRY block skips it entirely.
